themes.name: The fear of the LORD
themes.line: Where the book says wisdom begins: reverence for the LORD, and what it does in a life.

note.title: The fear of the LORD
note.body: The book's foundation, stated at 1:7 and again at 9:10, is reverent awe toward the LORD, the God of Israel. This fear isn't terror but a settled recognition of who God is, which shows itself in humility, obedience, and turning from evil. Wisdom in Proverbs is never simply shrewdness; it grows from this root, and the book returns to it at its close in the praise of a woman who fears the LORD.

themes.name: Wisdom and her call
themes.line: Wisdom calling in the streets, her worth above silver and gold, and her place beside God when he made the world.

note.title: Wisdom personified
note.body: In chapters 1, 8, and 9, wisdom speaks as a woman who calls in public places, offers life and favor, and was present with God when he made the world. Her rival, Folly, also calls to passers-by. The personification makes the choice concrete and personal: to choose wisdom is to accept an invitation to a relationship, not only to master a set of rules.

themes.name: The two ways
themes.line: The path of the righteous and the path of the wicked, and where each one ends.

note.title: Two ways
note.body: Proverbs pictures life as a road with two paths: the way of wisdom and righteousness, which leads to life, and the way of folly and wickedness, which leads to death. Choices that look small, a companion, a loan, a glance, a lie, set a person on one road or the other. The book trains the reader to see where a path ends before stepping onto it.

themes.name: The LORD who sees and directs
themes.line: The plans people make, and the LORD who weighs hearts, directs steps and has the last word.

themes.name: Listening, correction and counsel
themes.line: Receiving instruction, taking a rebuke, and seeking many counselors before a plan.

themes.name: The fool, the mocker and the simple
themes.line: The people Proverbs warns about, and the same tendencies in the reader: the closed mind, the scornful one and the easily led.

themes.name: Words and the tongue
themes.line: Honest and lying lips, gentle and harsh answers, gossip, flattery, and the wisdom of holding your tongue.

note.title: Words and speech
note.body: Few subjects get more attention in Proverbs than the tongue. The book contrasts honest and lying lips, gentle and harsh answers, gossip and discretion, flattery and faithful rebuke. Words build up or tear down a household and a city, and restraint in speech is repeatedly treated as a mark of wisdom.

themes.name: Anger, quarrels and peace
themes.line: The hot temper and the slow one, how quarrels start and spread, and how they are calmed.

themes.name: Pride and humility
themes.line: Haughty eyes, being wise in your own eyes, and the humility that comes before honor.

themes.name: The heart
themes.line: The inner life Proverbs keeps returning to: joy and sorrow, hope deferred, a crushed spirit, and the heart the LORD searches.

themes.name: Friends, neighbors and companions
themes.line: The friend who loves at all times, the neighbor next door, and the company that shapes who you become.

themes.name: Parents and children
themes.line: A father's and a mother's teaching, the training and correcting of children, and the joy and grief children bring.

themes.name: Marriage and faithfulness
themes.line: The warnings against adultery, delight in the wife of your youth, the quarrelsome house, and the woman of noble character.

themes.name: Work and the slacker
themes.line: The diligent hand and the idle one, the ant at harvest, and the field gone to thorns.

note.title: Work, wealth, and the poor
note.body: Proverbs praises diligence and warns the sluggard, but it also warns against trusting riches, against dishonest gain, and against oppressing the poor. It says that the LORD defends the needy and that kindness to the poor is lending to God. Wealth is a real good in the book, but always a lesser one than wisdom, righteousness, and a good name.

themes.name: Wealth, poverty and generosity
themes.line: Riches and their limits, debt and putting up security, the poor man, and the open hand.

note.title: Work, wealth, and the poor
note.body: Proverbs praises diligence and warns the sluggard, but it also warns against trusting riches, against dishonest gain, and against oppressing the poor. It says that the LORD defends the needy and that kindness to the poor is lending to God. Wealth is a real good in the book, but always a lesser one than wisdom, righteousness, and a good name.

themes.name: Kindness and faithfulness
themes.line: Loving devotion and faithfulness, mercy to the needy, and good done to an enemy.

themes.name: Honest dealing
themes.line: Honest scales and unequal weights, bribes, fraud, and wealth gained too quickly.

themes.name: Justice, rulers and the king
themes.line: Kings and rulers, the courts and the witness stand, partiality, and the cause of the poor and the voiceless.

themes.name: Envy and revenge
themes.line: Envying the wicked, fretting over evildoers, gloating over an enemy, and leaving vengeance to the LORD.

themes.name: Wine, appetite and self-control
themes.line: Wine and strong drink, the glutton and the ruler's table, too much honey, and eyes that are never satisfied.

chapters.title: The Fear of the LORD and the Voice in the Street
chapters.summary: The book opens with a title and a statement of purpose: these proverbs are meant to give wisdom to the simple and the young and to add learning to the wise, beginning with the fear of the LORD. A father then warns his son not to join a gang that ambushes the innocent for plunder, and Wisdom, pictured as a woman, cries out in the city streets, warning those who refuse her that they will reap what they chose.

chapters.title: Search for Wisdom Like Hidden Treasure
chapters.summary: The father tells his son that if he searches for wisdom as eagerly as for silver, he will come to understand the fear of the LORD, because the LORD himself gives wisdom. That wisdom will protect him from two dangers: men who speak perversely and walk in darkness, and the forbidden woman who has abandoned her marriage covenant. The chapter ends by contrasting the upright, who remain in the land, with the wicked, who are uprooted from it.

chapters.title: Trust in the LORD with All Your Heart
chapters.summary: The father urges his son to keep his teaching, hold on to loving devotion and faithfulness, trust the LORD rather than his own understanding, honor God with his wealth, and accept the LORD's discipline as a sign of love. A hymn praises wisdom as more precious than silver and gold, a tree of life, and the means by which God made the world. The chapter closes with practical commands about treating neighbors rightly and a contrast between the LORD's curse on the wicked and his blessing on the righteous.

chapters.title: Get Wisdom, Guard Your Heart
chapters.summary: The father passes on what his own father taught him: get wisdom, love her, and she will protect and honor you. He then contrasts the path of the righteous, which grows brighter like the dawn, with the dark way of the wicked, who cannot sleep until they have done harm. Finally he urges his son to guard his heart, his speech, his eyes, and his steps, and not to swerve from the straight path.

chapters.title: Drink Water from Your Own Cistern
chapters.summary: The father warns his son that the forbidden woman's words are sweet as honey at first but bitter as wormwood in the end, leading down to death. Going to her costs a man his strength, his years, and his wealth, and leaves him at life's end groaning with regret. Instead, the son should find joy and delight in his own wife, knowing that the LORD sees every path and that a man's own sins become the cords that trap him.

chapters.title: The Pledge, the Ant, and Seven Things the LORD Hates
chapters.summary: The father warns his son to free himself quickly from a rash pledge made for someone else's debt, urges the lazy to learn from the ant, and describes the worthless man who stirs up trouble with twisted speech and gestures. A numerical saying lists seven things the LORD hates. The chapter closes with another warning against adultery, which, unlike theft driven by hunger, brings disgrace and a jealous husband's fury that no payment can settle.

chapters.title: A Young Man at Twilight
chapters.summary: The father urges his son to treasure his commandments and to call wisdom his sister, so that he will be kept from the adulteress. Then he tells what he saw from his window: a young man without sense wandering near a woman's house at dusk, met by her in the street, persuaded by her invitation while her husband is away, and following her like an ox to the slaughter. The chapter ends by warning that her house is the road to Sheol.

chapters.title: Wisdom Calls: I Was There When He Made the World
chapters.summary: Wisdom stands at the crossroads and the city gates and calls to all people, promising truth, righteousness, and riches better than gold. She says that kings rule and princes govern justly by her, and that she loves those who love her. Then she describes her origin: the LORD brought her forth before the world began, and she was at his side as he set the heavens, the seas, and the foundations of the earth, rejoicing in his world and in humanity. Whoever finds her finds life; whoever hates her loves death.

chapters.title: Two Houses, Two Feasts
chapters.summary: Wisdom builds a house with seven pillars, prepares a banquet of meat and mixed wine, and sends her servants to invite the simple to leave folly and live. A short interlude contrasts the mocker, who hates correction, with the wise, who grow wiser when rebuked, and repeats that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. Then Folly, loud and ignorant, calls to the same passers-by from her doorway, promising that stolen water is sweet; but her guests are in the depths of Sheol.

chapters.title: The Proverbs of Solomon Begin: Two Ways in Two Lines
chapters.summary: A new heading, “The proverbs of Solomon”, opens the book's largest collection. The long poems of chapters 1 to 9 give way to short, self-contained sayings, most of them two lines that set the righteous against the wicked and the wise against the fool. This first chapter gathers sayings on work and harvest, on wealth gained honestly or dishonestly, and above all on speech: lips, mouth, and tongue that either give life or conceal violence.

chapters.title: Honest Scales, Generous Hands, and a City's Health
chapters.summary: The chapter opens in the marketplace, with the LORD's hatred of dishonest scales, and moves through pride and humility, the ruin that wickedness brings on itself, the effect of the righteous and the wicked on a whole city, and the uses of wealth. Generosity that seems to lose ends up gaining, hoarding that seems to gain ends up cursed, and the chapter closes with a tree of life and a warning that all receive their due.

chapters.title: Loving Correction, Tending the Land, Guarding the Tongue
chapters.summary: The chapter begins with a blunt saying: whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, and whoever hates correction is stupid. From there it gathers sayings on a good wife and a shameful one, the stability of the righteous household, care for animals, honest work on the land, and, above all, words: lying lips and truthful ones, rash speech that wounds and wise speech that heals. It closes on the path of righteousness, where there is life.

chapters.title: Hope Deferred, Honest Gain, and a Father's Discipline
chapters.summary: The chapter weaves together a wise son who listens, guarded speech, wealth gained slowly or dishonestly, and the long view of an inheritance left to grandchildren. It contains one of the Bible's most honest lines about longing (verse 12), and it closes with the saying that the one who spares the rod hates his son, followed by a picture of the righteous who have enough and the wicked who go hungry.

chapters.title: The Wise Woman's House and the Way That Seems Right
chapters.summary: A wise woman builds her house and a foolish one tears it down, and from there the chapter ranges widely: the simple who believe everything and the prudent who watch their steps, the heart's hidden bitterness and joy, a way that seems right but ends in death, the poor and their Maker, the king and his people, and the righteousness that exalts a nation. Running through it is the fear of the LORD as a fountain of life and a place of refuge.

chapters.title: A Gentle Answer and the LORD Who Sees
chapters.summary: The chapter opens with a gentle answer that turns away wrath and keeps returning to the tongue: soothing or perverse, timely or rash. Alongside speech it sets the LORD, who sees every place, weighs sacrifice and prayer, knows the depths of Sheol and of the human heart, and defends the widow's boundaries. Two better-than sayings prize a little with love and the fear of the LORD over plenty with turmoil, and the final verse joins the fear of the LORD to humility.

chapters.title: The Heart Plans, the LORD Directs
chapters.summary: The chapter opens with the densest group of sayings about the LORD in the whole collection: people make plans, weigh their own motives, and cast lots, but the LORD weighs hearts, establishes steps, and decides outcomes. A matching group of sayings follows on the king, whose justice and favor mirror God's rule. The rest of the chapter gathers famous sayings on pride before a fall, pleasant words, gray hair as a crown, and the patient person who is better than a warrior.

chapters.title: Quiet Crusts, Tested Hearts, and a Friend for Adversity
chapters.summary: The chapter prefers a dry crust in peace to a feast full of strife, and it moves through the LORD's testing of hearts, mockery of the poor, the workings of bribery, the damage of quarrels, and the grief of a foolish son. Its best known lines praise the friend who loves at all times and the brother born for adversity, and it ends with the observation that even a fool seems wise when he keeps quiet.

chapters.title: The Strong Tower and the Power of the Tongue
chapters.summary: The chapter begins with the person who cuts himself off from others and the fool who only wants to air his opinions. It sets the name of the LORD, a strong tower for the righteous, beside the rich man's imagined fortress, and gathers sayings on hasty answers, lawsuits, gifts, offended brothers, and a wife as a good gift. At its center is the claim that life and death are in the power of the tongue, and it closes with the friend who sticks closer than a brother.

chapters.title: Friends of the Rich, a Loan to the LORD
chapters.summary: The chapter returns again and again to the poor: better poor with integrity than a fool, deserted by friends and brothers, yet so close to God that kindness to them is a loan to the LORD. Around that theme it gathers sayings on false witnesses, the king's anger and favor, foolish sons and quarrelsome wives, a prudent wife as the LORD's gift, the discipline of children, and the plans of the human heart set beside the purpose of the LORD that stands.

chapters.title: Wine, Weights, and the Lamp of the LORD
chapters.summary: The chapter opens with wine as a mocker and moves through a wide range of daily matters: the king's terror and justice, the slacker who does not plow, the hidden purposes of the heart, haggling buyers, collateral for loans, rash vows, and differing weights that the LORD detests. At its heart are sayings that humble every reader: no one can claim a pure heart, a person's steps are from the LORD, and the human spirit is the lamp of the LORD searching the inmost being.

chapters.title: The King's Heart in the LORD's Hand
chapters.summary: The chapter opens with the king's heart as a channel of water that the LORD directs wherever he pleases, and it closes with the reminder that no wisdom or plan prevails against the LORD and that victory belongs to him even when the war horse is ready. Between those frames it prizes justice above sacrifice, warns against haste, lying, pleasure, and greed, laments a contentious home, and contrasts the craving slacker with the righteous who give without holding back.

chapters.title: A Good Name, a Child's Way, and the Words of the Wise
chapters.summary: The first sixteen verses close the long collection of Solomon's proverbs with sayings on a good name, the rich and poor who share one Maker, training a child, debt, generosity, and the oppression of the poor. At verse 17 a new voice begins: the words of the wise, a collection of longer sayings introduced with a call to listen and a promise of thirty sayings, which warns against robbing the poor, befriending the hot-tempered, pledging for debts, and moving ancient boundary stones.

chapters.title: At the Ruler's Table and the Drunkard's Cup
chapters.summary: The words of the wise continue with warnings about the table of a ruler and of a stingy host, the fleeting nature of wealth, and moving a boundary stone to steal from orphans. A father pleads with his son to be wise, to shun gluttony, drunkenness, and the prostitute, and the chapter closes with a vivid, almost comic portrait of a man ruined by wine who can't wait for his next drink.

chapters.title: Rescue the Perishing, and the Slacker's Field
chapters.summary: The words of the wise conclude with sayings about envy of the wicked, the house that wisdom builds, the duty to rescue those being led to death, and the danger of gloating over a fallen enemy. A second short collection, also called sayings of the wise, adds counsel on fair judgment, honest words, and refusing revenge, and ends with a scene: a teacher walks past a neglected field and draws a lesson about laziness.

chapters.title: Proverbs Copied by Hezekiah's Men
chapters.summary: A new collection of Solomon's proverbs begins, copied by the scribes of King Hezekiah. It opens with sayings about God, kings, and conduct at court, then offers a gallery of comparisons drawn from weather, jewelry, food, and daily life, on words well spoken, restraint, false witness, and self-control, including the command to feed a hungry enemy.

chapters.title: Fools, Slackers, and Smooth Talkers
chapters.summary: Three portraits dominate this chapter. The first twelve verses describe the fool, who should not be honored or trusted with a message and who returns to his folly like a dog to its vomit. Verses 13 to 16 mock the slacker, and verses 17 to 28 expose the meddler, the gossip, the quarreler, and the hateful man who hides malice behind gracious speech.

chapters.title: Friends, Tomorrow, and the Care of the Flock
chapters.summary: This chapter gathers sayings on humility about the future, on the value of honest friends and honest rebuke, on neighbors and family, on prudence, and on the restless human appetite. It closes with a short poem urging the reader to know the condition of his flocks and herds, because wealth and even crowns do not last, while faithful work provides for a household.

chapters.title: The Righteous Are Bold as a Lion
chapters.summary: This chapter contrasts the wicked and the righteous in public life, especially in how rulers treat the poor. It praises those who keep God's law, commends integrity over wealth, and warns against greed, partiality, and flattery. At its center is one of the Bible's clearest sayings on confession: the one who conceals sin will not prosper, but the one who confesses and renounces it will find mercy.

chapters.title: When the Righteous Flourish, the People Rejoice
chapters.summary: The Hezekiah collection closes with sayings about how rulers shape a people, how discipline shapes a child, and how anger, pride, and flattery shape a life. It warns that the fear of man is a snare and ends by reminding readers that true justice comes from the LORD and that the righteous and the wicked find each other detestable.

chapters.title: The Words of Agur: Humble Wisdom and Numbered Wonders
chapters.summary: An otherwise unknown sage named Agur confesses his weariness and ignorance before God, asks who has ascended to heaven, and affirms that every word of God is flawless. He prays for neither poverty nor riches, then offers a series of observations, many arranged in numbered lists, on arrogant generations, insatiable things, wonders he cannot understand, things that upset the social order, small but wise creatures, and stately walkers.

chapters.title: A Mother's Counsel and the Woman of Valor
chapters.summary: King Lemuel records his mother's teaching: a king must not waste his strength on women or dull his judgment with wine, and he must speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves. The book then closes with an acrostic poem praising a wife of noble character, strong, industrious, generous, and wise, whose worth lies above all in her fear of the LORD.

reading: Read Proverbs as proverbs. A proverb is a compressed observation about how life usually goes under God, not a promise or a guarantee for every case. “Idle hands make one poor, but diligent hands bring wealth” (10:4) is true as a pattern, and the book knows it has exceptions: it speaks of the poor who are oppressed and of wicked men who prosper for a time. The clearest signal is 26:4-5, where two proverbs placed side by side give opposite advice about answering a fool. Wisdom lies in knowing which one fits the moment. The same applies to sayings like 22:6 on training a child: they describe the normal fruit of faithful parenting, not a contract that makes parents solely responsible for a grown child's choices.

Watch for the two paths and the two women, Wisdom and Folly, that frame the book's opening; for the recurring figures of the simple, the fool, the mocker, the sluggard, and the righteous; and for parallelism, where the second line of a saying repeats, contrasts with, or extends the first. Read the sayings slowly and a few at a time. Many readers take one chapter a day, which fits a book of thirty-one chapters.

verses.t: Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you yourself will be like him.
Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he become wise in his own eyes.

pair.q: Verses 4 and 5 give opposite advice. Is the Bible contradicting itself?
a: Verse 4 says not to answer a fool according to his folly, or you will become like him. Verse 5 says to answer a fool according to his folly, or he will become wise in his own eyes. The collectors placed these sayings next to each other on purpose, and ancient Jewish interpreters already discussed the tension. The most common reading is that both are true in different situations: sometimes engaging a fool on his own terms drags you down to his level, and sometimes silence lets his folly stand unchallenged. Others suggest the two verses address different aspects of an answer, refusing to adopt the fool's manner (verse 4) while exposing his argument on its own terms (verse 5).

Either way, the pair teaches how to read the whole book. A proverb describes how life usually goes, not a guarantee or a rule for every case. Wisdom is the ability to judge which proverb fits the moment, a skill that no single saying can supply.
